blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

A tree is a recursive structure: a node whose children are themselves trees. That is why nearly every tree problem has a short **recursive** solution, and why the key skill is deciding *what each call returns*.

Two traversals cover everything:

- **Depth-first (DFS)** goes down a path before trying siblings. The order in which you touch the node gives **preorder** (node, left, right), **inorder** (left, node, right; sorted order for a BST) and **postorder** (left, right, node; children are known before the parent, so it suits "compute from the bottom up").
- **Breadth-first (BFS)** visits level by level using a queue. Use it for level order, right side view, and shortest distance in an unweighted tree.
"depth", "height", "balanced", "ancestor", "path sum", "level", "BST", "serialize". For a **BST**, think inorder = sorted, and use the ordering to discard half of the tree at every step.
blocks.title: Signal words

blocks.text:
The pattern for bottom-up problems (diameter, maximum path sum, balanced tree) is: **return one thing to the parent, record another thing globally**. For the diameter, a node returns its *height* to the parent but updates the best *diameter* (left height + right height) through itself.

| Question | Approach | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Height, depth, same tree, invert | Recursion, postorder | O(n) time, O(h) stack |
| Level order, right side view | BFS with a queue | O(n) time, O(w) queue |
| Validate BST | Pass `(lo, hi)` bounds down | O(n) |
| LCA in a BST | Walk down using the ordering | O(h) |

Here *h* is the height of the tree: O(log n) when balanced and O(n) when it degenerates into a list.

blocks.title: TreeTemplates.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** `isValidBST` passes `long` bounds because a node may legitimately hold `Integer.MIN_VALUE` or `MAX_VALUE`. Checking only each node against its direct children is the classic wrong answer: a deep right descendant can still be smaller than the root.

- **Checking only parent and child** for a BST instead of carrying bounds.
- **Recursion depth.** A degenerate tree of 100,000 nodes overflows the Java stack with recursion. Mention an iterative traversal with an explicit stack.
- **Mixing "return" and "record"**: a function that returns the height cannot also return the diameter; use a holder such as `int[]` or a field.
- **Forgetting the null base case**, which is also the most common source of `NullPointerException`.
- **BFS level size**: read `queue.size()` *before* the inner loop, because the queue grows during it.

O(h) for the call stack, where h is the height: O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) in the worst case of a skewed tree. BFS needs O(w) for the queue, where w is the widest level, which can be about n/2 for a complete tree.
blocks.title: Interview angle: What is the space complexity of recursive DFS on a tree?
Key points
blocks.text:
- Tree problems are recursive: decide what each call returns
- Preorder, inorder (sorted for a BST) and postorder (bottom-up) are the DFS orders
- BFS with a queue gives level order; read the queue size before the level loop
- Bottom-up problems return one value and record another
- Validate a BST with bounds, not with parent-child checks
- Recursion depth is O(h); mention an iterative version for skewed trees

blocks.title: Practise and track them
blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **Trees** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

items.question: Why does inorder traversal of a BST give sorted output?
items.answer: At every node the left subtree holds smaller values and the right subtree larger ones. Inorder visits left, node, right, so values come out in increasing order.

items.question: Why is checking `node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val` not enough to validate a BST?
items.answer: It misses violations from further down: a node in the right subtree of the root's left child can be larger than the root and still satisfy its own parent. You must carry the (low, high) bounds inherited from all ancestors.

items.question: How do you compute the diameter in O(n)?
items.answer: Do one postorder traversal where each node returns its height to the parent and updates a global maximum with `leftHeight + rightHeight`. Computing heights separately for every node would be O(n²) on a skewed tree.
